name: dff-lock
metrics: latency 6 gt, edge rising, setup 1 gt, hold 1 gt
caption: D flip-flop, 9 blocks: the data runs through two repeaters, and each has a lock repeater beside it (a locked repeater holds its output). The master's lock reads the clock block itself, so the first repeater follows d only while the clock is LOW; a wall torch hanging on that same clock block feeds the slave's lock, so the second repeater passes only while the clock is HIGH. On the rising edge the master freezes on d and the slave opens: q takes d exactly at the edge. No clock wiring at all: the clock block is part of the circuit.

name: dffe-lock
metrics: latency 6 gt, edge rising
caption: D flip-flop with enable, 12 blocks: the 9-block flip-flop (two repeaters with lock repeaters beside them; the master's lock reads the clock block, a wall torch on that block feeds the slave's) plus one more lock on the slave's other side, fed by a wall torch on the enable block. A repeater is locked if EITHER side is powered, so while e is off the slave stays locked through any clock edge and q holds; no AND gate is needed.

name: shift2-lock
metrics: N 2, latency 6 gt, edge rising

The first stage reads the clock block directly (its master lock behind it, its slave's wall torch hanging on it); a dust on top of the clock block carries the clock round to the second stage's stone, which plays the same part for it. name: tffr-ring

caption: T flip-flop with reset, 7 blocks: two droppers and two hoppers in a ring pass one stone around, and a comparator reading the second dropper is the output. A t pulse fires both droppers; only the one holding the stone moves it, into a hopper that hands it on 8 ticks later, after both droppers have fired, so q toggles. One dust on the first hopper, under the t input block, fires both droppers at once: it points into the cells above them, and a dropper also fires on power in the cell above it. An r pulse fires the second dropper alone: if it holds the stone, the stone leaves and q clears; otherwise nothing moves.

caption: Gives 64 output pulses (2 ticks on, one every 4 ticks) for each input, and stays 25 blocks for any count: the count is the number of items in a dropper (61 items for 64 pulses, up to 579 pulses with 9 full stacks). Details: the input cell is a copper bulb; its comparator and an observer give one pulse per input rising edge, which toggles a second bulb on. The comparator reading that bulb locks the return hopper and powers a sticky piston that pushes an observer face to face with another, and the pair fires the dropper every 4 ticks, one item into the hopper each time; the other observer's back is the output. When the dropper is empty, its comparator turns off and the torch on its output block lights, toggling the bulb off: the piston pulls the observer away and the hopper returns the items, 8 ticks each.

name: sorter-classic
metrics: items/s 2.50, first item by 20 gt, hoppers awake 2, badges tileable+overflow, bill 15 iron, 1 quartz, 10 redstone
caption: Takes one item kind out of a line of mixed items into its chest, 15 blocks a slice: slices stand side by side, one kind each, at full hopper speed (2.5 items/s), and a full chest never jams the line or drains a neighbour. Recipe (every item is required, none is a test load: 105 iron ingots and 8 papers in all): the filter hopper (under the line hopper) gets 41 of the item to sort in its first slot and 1 paper renamed "filter" in each of its 4 other slots (any item that never comes down the line); the drain hopper under it gets 64 of the item in its first slot and 4 items that cannot stack with the filter's fillers (here papers renamed "lock"). 16-stack items (snowballs, ender pearls): 10 in the filter and 16 in the drain, the same fillers (designs/circuits/tracks/sorter/sorter-classic-16.txt, also judged with both badges). It cannot sort non-stackable items (tools, armour: they pass through) nor items whose name or enchantments differ from the recipe's. How it works: one more item in the filter raises its comparator signal from 2 to 3, the only level that gets through three dust to the repeater, which powers the torch's block; the torch (hung under the comparator's block, which locks the drain) turns off, and the full drain drops one item into the chest and takes one from the filter. Catalog parts: the NOT gate (a torch on a block) as the lock, a 2 gt repeater.

name: lock1-hid
metrics: dials 1, combinations tried 16 (8 per code, 2 codes), opens within 6 gt, closes within 8 gt
caption: Put any item in each of the 2 item frames; a frame turns through 8 positions, one right-click each. The 1 dial hang on the front (west) face; the code frames hang on the back (east) face, facing away, so a player at the dials sees only the dials and the output, never the code. Set the code from behind by turning the code frames, then turn the dials to match them: the torch at the north end, under the bus, lights (open) only when every dial shows the same position as its code frame, and never for a moment while you turn. Wire a piston door or an iron door to that torch. Inside, per dial: a comparator behind the code frame's block reads the code and powers a block beside the code dust, so the dust carries the code at full value; the dial's comparator passes the dial's value only if it is at least the code (else a torch under its dust lights), and a second comparator passes the code only if it is at least the dial's value (else a torch on its block lights). One dust line under all the torches joins every mismatch into the block under its north end, which turns the output torch off (opens within 6 ticks, closes within 8). A dial takes 3 rows; dials pair up back to back, with one empty row between pairs.

name: seven-segment-rings5
metrics: latency 70 gt (a0 falls from a=0011), glitches 29
caption: A hex 7-segment display: set the four input levers to a value 0-15 and the seven lamps on the front face show its digit (0-9, then A b C d E F). Inside, the four bits become one signal strength (a chain of four subtract comparators reading composters; the faster inputs' repeaters are slowed so every bit arrives in the same tick), carried over comparator lines to seven rings of comparators, one per segment, stacked in three towers behind and beside the face. Each ring's comparators each pass one range of strengths (a hopper sets the range; a second comparator gives the lower edge), the ring's centre dust is lit when any of them passes, and a repeater lane carries it to the segment's lamp. Only the top ring of each tower has its own line: the rings below read the strength through the blocks the ring above powers right over them, and each ring keeps only the dust and bridges its comparators need.

name: seven-segment-therm-v11
metrics: latency 86 gt (a0 rises from a=0000)
caption: A 7-segment display: four input lines (a 4-bit number) light the seven lamps of a readable digit on its front face, 0-9 then A b C d E F, with no flicker while the number changes (glitch-free). A chain of subtract comparators turns the four bits into one signal strength; four shared dust rulers give every threshold (two segments per ruler where they fit); each run of values a segment lights is one subtract comparator between two taps of the same ruler; routed repeater lanes carry each segment to its lamp, with the inputs' delays equalised so every change arrives in the same tick. Catalog parts: comparator gates, repeater delays.
